title: Sampling Distribution of a Proportion
short: Sample proportions center on p with spread √(p(1 − p)/n).
trouble: Students confuse the distribution of one sample's data with the distribution of the statistic.

blocks.html: Poll 1,000 voters and 52% support a measure; poll another 1,000 and you might get 49%. The sample proportion $\hat{p}$ is itself a random variable. Its distribution over all possible samples, the sampling distribution, follows from the binomial distribution and is close to a normal curve. You saw this kind of variation in simulations.

For random samples of size $n$ from a population with proportion $p$, the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ has
$$\mu_{\hat{p}} = p, \qquad \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}.$$
When $np \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p) \ge 10$, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal.

The number of successes $X$ in the sample is binomial (when the population is large, or at least 10 times the sample), with mean $np$ and SD $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$. Since $\hat{p} = X/n$, divide both by $n$: the mean becomes $p$ and the SD becomes $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}/n = \sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$. With enough expected successes and failures, the binomial bars fill in a bell shape, so a normal curve fits.

blocks.name: sampling
blocks.cap: Each sample gives one proportion of heads. Take 1,000 samples, then move n: the proportions always center on 0.5, and their spread shrinks like 1/√n.

blocks.title: Center and spread
blocks.q: 40% of a city's adults have a library card. For random samples of 150 adults, describe the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$.
steps: Shape: $np = 60$ and $n(1 - p) = 90$ are both at least 10, so approximately normal.

blocks.title: A probability
blocks.q: In that setting, how likely is a sample with $\hat{p} \ge 0.48$? ($P(Z < 2.00) = 0.9772$.)
blocks.a: About $0.023$: a sample this high would be unusual.

blocks.title: A bigger sample
blocks.q: What happens to $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ with samples of 600 instead of 150?
steps: n is 4 times as large, so $\sigma_{\hat{p}}$ is divided by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

blocks.html: Confusing the distribution of one sample's data with the distribution of the statistic. One sample's data are just yeses and nos (0s and 1s); they are not bell-shaped at all. The bell shape describes $\hat{p}$ across many different samples. Check: is the question about individuals, or about a statistic computed from a whole sample?
